narrative:
The 2020 Texas Rangers entered the pandemic-shortened 60-game season with cautious optimism, but the campaign quickly revealed a team short on pitching and inconsistent at the plate. Playing in a bubble-style environment with no fans in Globe Life Field — their brand-new ballpark — the Rangers stumbled to a 2-4 record in July, setting a troubling early tone. The offense showed flashes, most notably Joey Gallo and Elvis Andrus combining for a dramatic late-game rally on July 29th, but the pitching staff was already leaking runs at an alarming rate.

August was the Rangers' best month, yet even a 10-17 record felt like treading water. The rotation cycled through its share of disasters — Kyle Gibson surrendered grand slams on back-to-back days against San Diego, and Rafael Montero handed Manny Machado a grand slam that swung an entire game in an instant. Against those dark moments, the team found occasional sparks: Nick Solak hit a clutch home run, Danny Santana delivered a key two-run double, and Gallo continued his power surge with his seventh homer of the year on August 19th. Still, the gap between runs scored and runs allowed told the real story — the bullpen and rotation were simply not good enough to compete.

September offered no salvation. The Rangers went 10-17 again, mirroring their August futility. Nick Goody surrendered a devastating three-run homer to Michael Brantley in early September, a -0.531 WPA gut-punch that became emblematic of the bullpen's inability to protect leads. Joey Gallo provided one of the season's brightest individual moments with a ground-rule double on September 16th, and Ronald Guzman closed out the year with a solo shot that at least gave the team something to cheer about in the final days. But by then, the Rangers were already eliminated, watching younger teams chase playoff spots.

Finishing 22-38, the Rangers ranked among the worst teams in baseball, surrendering 312 runs against only 224 scored. The 5.02 ERA told a damning story about a pitching staff that was never able to keep the team in games, while a .649 OPS offense rarely gave its pitchers any margin for error. The season served as a painful reminder that the franchise was still in rebuilding mode, even as the new ballpark gleamed in Arlington — a monument to a future that had not yet arrived.

chapters.title: Opening Day Dramatics
chapters.description: The Rangers kick off the shortened season with a wild, back-and-forth game that showcases both their offensive firepower and defensive vulnerabilities.

chapters.title: Pitching Unravels
chapters.description: The Rangers' rotation begins to crack as opposing hitters punish a thin pitching staff, turning winnable games into losses.

chapters.title: Winning Ugly in August
chapters.description: Despite a series of crushing home runs allowed, the Rangers scrape together their best month, staying afloat on clutch hits from Gallo, Solak, and Santana.

chapters.title: September Fade
chapters.description: Any remaining playoff hope evaporates as the bullpen collapses and the offense goes quiet, leaving only individual bright spots in an otherwise forgettable final month.

chapters.title: Guzman's Farewell Salute
chapters.description: Ronald Guzman punctuates a lost season with a memorable late home run, offering a rare moment of joy as the Rangers play out the string.
